# Owner interaction preferences

Personal preferences from the repo owner for how the assistant should interact — tone, summary style, end-of-turn conventions, how results and decisions are surfaced, and the phrases the owner uses to trigger defined commands. These are **not** project conventions (those live in the [packs/](https://github.com/missingbulb/Claudinite/tree/main/packs) corpus, each pack bundling its skills); they're how the owner likes to be worked with. Where a preference triggers a command whose mechanics are a project convention, the mechanics stay in their own doc and the entry here just owns the trigger phrase.

## Preferences

- **End every turn with a blockquote callout** — `> ✅ All done`, or `> ⚠️ Still open: …` listing what remains — never hedged in prose.
- **"LGTM"** merges the change at hand into `main` (`merge-to-main` skill); it approves that change only, never later work.
- **"bump version"** raises the project's version; the project's own workflow decides how it changes and which files change.
- **In the conversation**: link every source-controlled document you edit, display every image you edit, link every issue/PR number.
- **Ask every decision or approval through an `AskUserQuestion` popup, never prose** — one question per item, each with its case.
- **Enclose anything the owner will lift elsewhere** — a prompt, a message, copy to paste — in one delimited block, boundaries unmistakable.
- **Prefix a prompt for another session, inside its block, with a disclaimer**: Claude wrote it — examine inconsistencies, don't follow blindly.
- **Open a pull request right after committing to a branch**, unasked — overriding Claude Code's default of waiting to be told.
- **When handing over a PR to review, describe the folders the change touched in the conversation, in a text box** — a brief line per folder saying what changed there. Show non-test folders only, and ignore README files, comment-only changes, and history-keeping updates (a version bump, a changelog or `VERSIONS.md` row).
- **Keep working through a multi-step plan without pausing for approval of each step** — aggregate the steps into one substantial change to review, and stop only for an action that reaches the world (a release, a fleet-wide effect, anything irreversible) or a decision only the owner can make.
- **Never schedule a self check-in to poll a PR** — no recurring wake-up, routine, or `send_later` re-arm that re-reads a PR's state, CI or mergeability on a timer. Act on PR events when they arrive; when nothing has arrived, end the turn.

Environment setup incomplete: Node dependencies (npm ci) is not installed. Alert the user: re-paste the full body of the setup script (`find .claudinite/shared -name environment-setup-command.sh`; a pack owns it, so the engine does not name its path) into the Claude Code Web environment Setup script field (environment settings), then start a fresh session so the snapshot rebuilds with the prerequisites installed.

## github
The GitHub MCP Server provides tools to interact with GitHub platform.

Tool selection guidance:
	1. Use 'list_*' tools for broad, simple retrieval and pagination of all items of a type (e.g., all issues, all PRs, all branches) with basic filtering.
	2. Use 'search_*' tools for targeted queries with specific criteria, keywords, or complex filters (e.g., issues with certain text, PRs by author, code containing functions).

Context management:
	1. Use pagination whenever possible with batches of 5-10 items.
	2. Use minimal_output parameter set to true if the full information is not needed to accomplish a task.

Tool usage guidance:
	1. For 'search_*' tools: Use separate 'sort' and 'order' parameters if available for sorting results - do not include 'sort:' syntax in query strings. Query strings should contain only search criteria (e.g., 'org:google language:python'), not sorting instructions. Always call 'get_me' first to understand current user permissions and context. ## Issues

Check 'list_issue_types' first for organizations to use proper issue types. Use 'search_issues' before creating new issues to avoid duplicates. Always set 'state_reason' when closing issues. ## Pull Requests

PR review workflow: Always use 'pull_request_review_write' with method 'create' to create a pending review, then 'add_comment_to_pending_review' to add comments, and finally 'pull_request_review_write' with method 'submit_pending' to submit the review for complex reviews with line-specific comments.

Before creating a pull request, search for pull request templates in the repository. Template files are called pull_request_template.md or they're located in '.github/PULL_REQUEST_TEMPLATE' directory. Use the template content to structure the PR description and then call create_pull_request tool.

- session-start-hook: Creating and developing startup hooks for Claude Code on the web. Use when the user wants to set up a repository for Claude Code on the web, create a SessionStart hook to ensure their project can run tests and linters during web sessions.
- adopt-claudinite: Bootstrap Claudinite into a consuming repo — mount, hooks, checks, skills. Use when asked to bootstrap, adopt, or set up Claudinite, or to baseline a repo to pick up updates.
- adopt-pack: Add one or more packs to an already-adopted Claudinite member — declare, run each pack's adoption interview, re-vendor, scaffold, land. Use when asked to adopt, add, enable, or declare a pack (e.g. product-wiki, executable-requirements) on a repo that already runs Claudinite.
- authoring-agent-docs: How to write instruction files coding agents follow reliably. Use before writing or editing any Claude instruction doc — a project CLAUDE.md, a convention doc, a routine spec.
- bug-investigation: Method for investigating a bug and pinning down its root cause. Use when investigating a bug report, when a fix didn't hold or a bug recurs, or when a report doesn't reproduce against main.
- ci-performance-evaluation: Method for finding where a repo's CI time actually goes and what is worth fixing. Use when CI feels slow, when investigating a runtime regression, or when the weekly ci-performance task hands you a finding.
- do-later: File a change to be made AFTER the work in flight — a well-defined issue, marked for the queue and blocked behind the current PR/issue and behind the previous deferral, so repeated asks chain. Use when the owner says "/do-later …", "do this after this lands", or otherwise defers a change instead of derailing the session.
- explore-link: Mine one given URL for product, market, usage and pricing insights and fold them into an existing product-wiki page — cited, dated, delivered as a PR. Use when the owner says "/explore-link <url>", or hands over a link and asks for it to be read into the wiki.
- extract-from-activity: Mine a window of a repo's commits, merged PRs and issue activity for durable, reusable lessons and land them in the repo's own local packs. Use when extracting lessons from repo artifacts — the growth-extract task's activity half, or an owner asking what a recent stretch of work taught.
- extract-from-conversations: Mine an agent-user conversation — a captured conversation log or the live session — for friction-driven lessons (misunderstandings, backtracks, measured wall-time waits) and land them in the repo's own local packs. Use when extracting lessons from a session transcript or the conversation-logs branch, or when an owner asks for a retrospective.
- file-placement: Where a file should live — the reference-distance metric, the high-reach code smell, and the mandated-location, test-location and plugin-contract exemptions. Use before placing, moving, or renaming a file, or when reviewing where one lives.
- git-github-advanced: Git/GitHub procedures beyond the baseline lifecycle. Use for commit layering, recovering a branch after a squash-merge, CI-trigger rules, GitHub Actions gotchas, or merge-relocation traps.
- github-actions-scheduling: What a GitHub Actions `schedule:` trigger actually guarantees — late fires, dropped fires, the 60-day disable — and how to build and describe scheduled work around it. Use when adding, changing, explaining, or debugging anything that runs on a cron in GitHub Actions.
- growth-dedup: Prune a repo's local packs of items the mounted Claudinite canon now covers — remove, strip to residue, or track a wording drift, never grow an entry. Use when the growth dedup task runs, or when asked to reconcile or dedup local packs against the canon.
- improve-comments: Improve the comments in a repo's own source — delete the ones that restate the code or narrate a past edit, correct the ones that have drifted from what the code now does, and add the why where only a reader's guess carries it. Use when working a repo's comments as their own pass (the tidy-repo pack's improve-comments task), never as a side effect of another change.
- map-a-data-source: Reconnaissance on a website you want data from but don't control — locate the real data surface (hydration blob, client API, or markup) and write the findings down before any parser exists. Use when adding a new source to a scraper, or when an existing source stops parsing and you suspect the site changed shape.
- merge-to-main: Merge the change in front of the owner into main. Use when the owner says "LGTM" or asks to merge/land the current branch or PR into main.
- production-retrospective: Design and file the review that comes back on its own once a larger element has lived in production long enough to judge — is it working, misused, overused, underused — read from its real production record against expectations written down when the element was designed. Use when designing a larger element (the brief is authored then), when filing a migration plan's chain (the retrospective is its last link), when a merge completes a design-doc'd element, or when defining a new retrospective class for a pack, a repo, or the fleet.
- prose-to-checks: Mine pack prose (RULES.md, SKILL.md) for always-testable rules that were never converted to checks, and convert the strongest ones. Use when auditing packs for convertible rules, when the weekly prose-to-checks sweep runs, or as the upgrade pass over prose a growth-extract run just wrote.
- repo-text-sweeps: Mechanics for grep/sed sweeps, renames, and path relocations across a repo. Use before a bulk find-replace, a rename, or moving files — and after one, to catch silently broken references.
- single-issue-triage: Triage one open issue and take the first applicable action — close-if-implemented, needs-decision, blocked, quick-win, or leave. Use when acting on a single issue; "implemented in main" must be verified against main's current content and the default is to comment, not close (e.g. the tidy-repo pack's tidy-issues task hands you issues to triage).
- single-pr-status: Assess one open pull request's landed status — keep-open, or closeable (merged, already-in-main, superseded, stale) — read-only. Use when triaging whether a single PR should stay open, judging by its commits and diff not its title (e.g. the tidy-repo pack's tidy-prs task hands you PRs to assess).
- unattended-agents: Architecture and practices for unattended, automation-invoked agents and recurring routines. Use when building, structuring, or running an AI agent, a scheduled routine, or a multi-stage agent pipeline.
- verify-in-production: Decide whether a change that has merged can only be proven in production, and if so file the verification that comes back on its own once it is live. Use immediately after the merge, beside the conversation capture — never before, and not on request.
- writing-handover-issues: How to write a task list a PERSON will execute — a handover issue, an adoption checklist, a "steps only a human can do" list. Use when filing or editing any issue whose body asks a human to click, set, register or copy something. Not for issues describing work you will do yourself.
- writing-migration-plans: Where a plan and a design live, and how to order a plan's phases so nothing stalls mid-run — the plan is a tracking issue (never a plan document in the repo), the design doc carries only the end state with rationale and alternatives; front-load the out-of-band setup, write ALL the code including the cleanup and take one approval for the stack, then chain every execution step to the verification of the one before it as a queued continuation, and keep the tracking issue append-only while implementing. Use BEFORE writing any DESIGN.md, migration plan, phased implementation plan, rollout or cutover plan — including the moment you are about to create a docs/<initiative>/ file — and when working through a plan's tracking issue.
- writing-pack-prose: How pack prose is written — RULES.md rules, SKILL.md bodies and check text in a Claudinite pack, local or canon — brevity, structure, triggerability, findability, and the per-pack references doc that carries each rule's rationale. Use before writing or editing any pack's RULES.md or SKILL.md, or when landing a lesson as prose.
- writing-tasks: The contract a Claudinite task is written to — the declaration's fields, the code-work and agentic phases, the precondition as the only decision point, ordering, and how a work item converges. Use when writing or changing a tasks/<name>/task.mjs or its worker, or when a task-declaration check fires.
- writing-tests: Practices for writing tests you can trust. Use before writing or changing any test — see-it-fail discipline, snapshot/golden rules, CI-only and heavy-browser tests, fuzzy-metric gating.
- design: Create a design canvas - a multi-artboard visual design published as an Artifact that runs Claude Design's canvas editor (an early preview of Claude Design inside Claude Code). You DRAFT the design as .dc.html artboards laid out on one pan/zoom canvas; where saving is enabled for the user's account they refine every element visually (click-to-select, a properties panel, inline text editing, undo/redo) and Save publishes a new version for everyone, otherwise they get a view-and-export (PNG/PDF) preview of your draft. Good for UI mockups and screen flows, landing pages, marketing and social graphics, and print pieces - posters, flyers, brochures as single-page artboards; memos and reports as one flowing artboard. Use when someone wants a design, mockup, wireframe, UI or screen design, landing page, poster, flyer, brochure, banner, card, one-pager, or any visual layout they would rather tweak by hand than in code. Only for CREATING or re-seeding a canvas; an existing one is edited in its published Artifact.
- dataviz: Use this skill whenever you are about to create ANY chart, graph, plot, dashboard, or data visualization, in ANY output medium — an HTML or React artifact, inline SVG, plotting code in any library (matplotlib, plotly, d3, Recharts, …), an image/PNG you will render and upload, or a chart shared into Slack. Read it BEFORE writing the first line of chart code, choosing chart colors, building a stat tile / meter / KPI row, or laying out a dashboard. When the destination is a first-party document connector (host-designated, never self-described) that renders live charts, hand it the rows (inline, or as an uploaded data file the chart cites) rather than a rendered PNG/SVG — a picture of a chart loses hover, data inspection and per-value comments. Produces visualizations that read as one system — elegant, accessible, consistent in light and dark — using a brand-neutral placeholder palette you swap for your own. Teaches a design-system-agnostic method: a form heuristic, a color formula with a runnable validator, mark specs, and interaction rules. A validated default palette is documented in `references/palette.md` — swap that file's values for your brand's. Triggers on: "chart", "graph", "plot", "data viz", "visualization", "dashboard", "analytics", "visualize data", "categorical colors", "sequential / diverging palette", "stat tile", "sparkline", "heatmap", "legend", "axis", "tooltip", "chart colors", "color by series".
- artifact-design: Design guidance and fundamentals for Artifacts. - Load before writing any artifact, including a skill-instructed Markdown one - Markdown is never a shortcut past the design pass.
- artifact-diagramming: Diagramming know-how for Artifacts - when a picture earns its place, how to draw one that shows the real mechanism, and the inline-SVG mechanics that keep it legible in both themes.
- artifact-capabilities: Runtime capabilities a published Artifact page can be granted — behavior static HTML cannot provide on its own, such as the page reading live or connected data, remembering what people do on it (a poll, a sign-up sheet, a checklist, a document edited in place — it saves new versions of itself), keeping state shared across viewers, knowing who is viewing, asking Claude a question of its own, storing files people add, or handing the viewer a file to save. Serves this user's live capability roster and the typed call definitions. Load it whenever the user asks for an artifact needing any such runtime behavior.
- update-config: Use this skill to configure the Claude Code harness via settings.json. Automated behaviors ("from now on when X", "each time X", "whenever X", "before/after X") require hooks configured in settings.json - the harness executes these, not Claude, so memory/preferences cannot fulfill them. Also use for: permissions ("allow X", "add permission", "move permission to"), env vars ("set X=Y"), hook troubleshooting, or any changes to settings.json/settings.local.json files. Examples: "allow npm commands", "add bq permission to global settings", "move permission to user settings", "set DEBUG=true", "when claude stops show X". For simple settings like theme/model, suggest the /config command.
- keybindings-help: Use when the user wants to customize keyboard shortcuts, rebind keys, add chord bindings, or modify ~/.claude/keybindings.json. Examples: "rebind ctrl+s", "add a chord shortcut", "change the submit key", "customize keybindings".
- code-review: Review the current diff, or a PR number/branch/path target, for correctness bugs and reuse/simplification/efficiency cleanups at the given effort level (low/medium: fewer, high-confidence findings; high→max: broader coverage, may include uncertain findings); with no level given, it reuses the level you typed last. Pass --comment to post findings as inline PR comments, or --fix to apply the findings to the working tree after the review.
- simplify: Review the changed code for reuse, simplification, efficiency, and altitude cleanups, then apply the fixes. Quality only — it does not hunt for bugs; use /code-review for that.
- fewer-permission-prompts: Scan your transcripts for common read-only Bash and MCP tool calls, then add a prioritized allowlist to project .claude/settings.json to reduce permission prompts.
- loop: Run a prompt or slash command on a recurring interval (e.g. /loop 5m /foo). Omit the interval to let the model self-pace. - When the user wants to set up a recurring task, poll for status, or run something repeatedly on an interval (e.g. "check the deploy every 5 minutes", "keep running /babysit-prs"). Do NOT invoke for one-off tasks.
- claude-api: Reference for the Claude API / Anthropic SDK — model ids, pricing, params, streaming, tool use, MCP, agents, caching, token counting, model migration.
TRIGGER — read BEFORE opening the target file; don't skip because it "looks like a one-liner" — whenever: the prompt names Claude/Anthropic in any form (Claude, Anthropic, Fable, Opus, Sonnet, Haiku, `anthropic`, `@anthropic-ai`, `claude-*`, `us.anthropic.*`, `[1m]`); the user asks about an LLM (pricing/model choice/limits/caching) — never answer from memory; OR the task is LLM-shaped with provider unstated (agent/MCP/tool-definition/multi-agent/RAG/LLM-judge/computer-use; generate/summarize/extract/classify/rewrite/converse over NL; debugging refusals/cutoffs/streaming/tool-calls/tokens).
SKIP only when another provider is being worked on (overrides all triggers): OpenAI/GPT/Gemini/Llama/Mistral/Cohere/Ollama named in the query; OR `grep -rE 'openai|langchain_openai|google.generativeai|genai|mistralai|cohere|ollama'` over the project hits (run this grep FIRST if no provider named — don't Read the file).
- workflow-authoring: Reference for writing a Workflow tool script (script API and gotchas, resume, quality patterns, worked examples). Load before authoring a script for a workflow the user already opted into; it does not itself authorize running one.
- run: Launch and drive this project's app to see a change working. Use when asked to run, start, or screenshot the app, or to confirm a change works in the real app (not just tests). First looks for a project skill that already covers launching the app; otherwise falls back to built-in patterns per project type (CLI, server, TUI, Electron, browser-driven, library).
- init: Initialize a new CLAUDE.md file with codebase documentation
- security-review: Complete a security review of the pending changes on the current branch
- docx: Use this skill whenever the user wants to create, read, edit, or manipulate Word documents (.docx) or Word templates (.dotx). Triggers include: any mention of 'Word doc', 'word document', '.docx', '.dotx', or requests to produce professional documents with formatting like tables of contents, page numbers, or letterheads. Also use when extracting or reorganizing content from .docx or .dotx files, inserting or replacing images in documents, find-and-replace in Word files, working with tracked changes or comments, or converting content into a polished Word document. If the user asks for a 'report', 'memo', 'letter', 'template', or similar deliverable as a Word or .docx file (to download, email or print), use this skill. However, if they ask for a document, page, report, memo, or notes WITHOUT naming a file format and the session offers a dedicated document or page skill or connector, use that instead. Do NOT use for PDFs, spreadsheets, Google Docs, or coding unrelated to document generation.
- import-memory: Import a memory export from another AI assistant into Claude's memory — conversationally, additively, and with the content treated as data.
- morning: Render the user's morning brief as a styled HTML artifact, or set it up as a recurring weekday task. Use only when the user explicitly asks to run, see, or set up their morning brief, or if they invoke /morning by name. A question about their day, schedule, or calendar is not by itself a request for the brief; answer it directly instead.
- pdf: Use this skill whenever the user wants to do anything with PDF files. This includes reading or extracting text/tables from PDFs, combining or merging multiple PDFs into one, splitting PDFs apart, rotating pages, adding watermarks, creating new PDFs, filling PDF forms, encrypting/decrypting PDFs, extracting images, and OCR on scanned PDFs to make them searchable. If the user mentions a .pdf file or asks to produce one, use this skill.
- pptx: Use this skill any time a .pptx or .potx file is involved in any way — as input, output, or both. This includes: creating slide decks, pitch decks, or presentations as PowerPoint (.pptx) files; reading, parsing, or extracting text from any .pptx or .potx file (even if the extracted content will be used elsewhere, like in an email, summary, or creating a different type of slide deck); editing, modifying, or updating existing presentations; combining or splitting slide files; working with templates (.potx), layouts, speaker notes, or comments. Trigger whenever the user asks for a PowerPoint or .pptx file, or references a .pptx or .potx filename, regardless of what they plan to do with the content afterward. However, when the user asks for a deck, slides, a slide deck, or a presentation without naming a file format, default to using a dedicated slide-deck artifact type or a separate slides skill if this session offers one; otherwise, use this skill.
- skill-creator: Create new skills, modify and improve existing skills, and measure skill performance. Use when users want to create a skill from scratch, edit, or optimize an existing skill, run evals to test a skill, benchmark skill performance with variance analysis, or optimize a skill's description for better triggering accuracy.
- xlsx: Use this skill any time a spreadsheet file is the primary input or output. This means any task where the user wants to: open, read, edit, or fix an existing .xlsx, .xlsm, .xltx, .csv, or .tsv file (e.g., adding columns, computing formulas, formatting, charting, cleaning messy data); create a new spreadsheet from scratch or from other data sources; or convert between tabular file formats. Trigger especially when the user references a spreadsheet file by name or path — even casually (like "the xlsx in my downloads") — and wants something done to it or produced from it. Also trigger for cleaning or restructuring messy tabular data files (malformed rows, misplaced headers, junk data) into proper spreadsheets. The deliverable must be a spreadsheet file. Do NOT trigger when the primary deliverable is a Word document, HTML report, standalone Python script, database pipeline, or Google Sheets API integration, even if tabular data is involved.

main = "src/backend/index.ts"
compatibility_date = "2026-08-01"

content.text:
{"number":27,"title":"Cloudflare provisioning for hitbut v1","body":"Phase 0 of #25. Production only: local development and the whole test suite run against wrangler's local D1/R2 and need none of this. **Rewritten 2026-08-23.** This list used to be nine dashboard steps and a two-pass first deploy. Most of that was never necessary — every resource is one non-interactive `wrangler … create`, and both deploy origins are readable off the deploys themselves. #69 landed the automation. **Two earlier comments on this issue carry checkboxes that are no longer steps** ([one](https://github.com/missingbulb/hitbut/issues/27#issuecomment-5373236216), [two](https://github.com/missingbulb/hitbut/issues/27#issuecomment-5376352028)). Everything still live in them is in this body; the `API_ORIGIN` variable is not a step at all any more. They are kept for the reasoning they record. **You never have to guess whether a step worked.** After each one run **[preflight](https://github.com/missingbulb/hitbut/actions/workflows/preflight.yml)** → *Run workflow*. It reads production and changes nothing, so run it as often as you like, and it names what is still missing and how to fix it. Read its output carefully: `MISS` means Cloudflare says the resource is not there, `??` means the question could not be asked at all (usually a token scope). They need opposite fixes — and the provisioner declines to create anything on a `??` for exactly that reason. --- ## A. The part that needs a person - [x] **Pick the Cloudflare account** and copy its Account ID — [dash.cloudflare.com](https://dash.cloudflare.com/) → any domain or *Workers & Pages*; the ID is in the right-hand sidebar (and it is the hex string in the dashboard URL, `dash.cloudflare.com//…`). - [x] **Create a scoped API token** — [dash.cloudflare.com/profile/api-tokens](https://dash.cloudflare.com/profile/api-tokens) → *Create Token* → *Create Custom Token*. - [x] **Paste both as repository secrets** — [Settings → Secrets → Actions](https://github.com/missingbulb/hitbut/settings/secrets/actions). ## B. Press the button - [x] **Run [provision](https://github.com/missingbulb/hitbut/actions/workflows/provision.yml)** → *Run workflow*. It creates every resource that is missing and leaves alone every one that is already there, so re-running it is safe and is the normal way to finish a partial run. [Run 32638007557](https://github.com/missingbulb/hitbut/actions/runs/32638007557) created the **D1 database** `hitbut-corpus`, created the **Pages project** `hitbut`, and pinned the real `database_id` into `wrangler.toml` on `main` (`0588653`). One resource is outstanding, below. ## B2. Outstanding: the R2 bucket - [ ] **R2 bucket `hitbut-raw`.** The provisioner could not *ask* whether it exists — `wrangler r2 bucket list` came back with `A request to the Cloudflare API (/accounts/…/r2/buckets) failed.` — so, correctly, it created nothing. A `??` is not a `MISS`.
*While off:* no raw-payload cache and no bulk NDJSON export; a parser fix would need a re-fetch. It is a **required** resource, so the deploy is gated on it. Two candidate causes, needing opposite fixes, and the run could not tell them apart because the error's second line was being dropped (fixed in #82): 1. **The token is missing R2 permission.** The one to add is *Account* → **Workers R2 Storage: Edit** — [edit the token](https://dash.cloudflare.com/profile/api-tokens), then re-paste it into [Actions secrets](https://github.com/missingbulb/hitbut/settings/secrets/actions) if you rolled it. 2. **R2 was never enabled on the account.** Unlike the other products, R2 has its own onboarding — [dash.cloudflare.com → R2](https://dash.cloudflare.com/?to=/:account/r2). If it shows a *Get started* / purchase screen rather than a bucket list, no token can list buckets until that is done, and this is a genuine dashboard step. **Do this:** open the R2 page above. If it needs onboarding, do that. Otherwise widen the token. Then re-run [provision](https://github.com/missingbulb/hitbut/actions/workflows/provision.yml) — once #82 lands, its failure message names the cause outright, and the run goes red rather than green if production still is not ready. ## B3. Waiting on the model choice, not on you - [ ] **Vectorize index `hitbut-utterances`.** Deliberately not created: an index fixes its dimension count at creation and the embedding model is not chosen (#34). Choose the model, set a `VECTORIZE_DIMENSIONS` [repository variable](https://github.com/missingbulb/hitbut/settings/variables/actions) to what it outputs, and re-run provision. Advisory until then — it does not block the deploy.
*While off:* ingestion has no retrieval step; nothing can be clustered or compared by position. ## C. Gate, then ship - [ ] **Run [preflight](https://github.com/missingbulb/hitbut/actions/workflows/preflight.yml) and get it green.** The deploy runs the same check before it touches anything, so a green preflight is the difference between a first deploy that works and one that fails halfway through having already deployed the Worker. - [ ] **Let a merge to `main` deploy.** One pass: preflight → migrations → Worker → site built against the origin the Worker just reported → site deployed → smoke test against both. No human step, which is requirement `7.1`. A custom domain in front of either half is the only thing that cannot be derived — set `API_ORIGIN` / `SITE_ORIGIN` as [repository variables](https://github.com/missingbulb/hitbut/settings/variables/actions) if you put one there, and they win. ## Not steps, contrary to what this issue used to say - **`API_ORIGIN` / `SITE_ORIGIN` as a required step** — #69 derives both off the deploys; they are custom-domain overrides now. - **Queue `hitbut-analysis`** — the queue was dropped in the redesign (#59); nothing binds one. - **Workers AI, Workflows** — neither has a binding in `wrangler.toml` today, so neither blocks anything until #34 lands the code that uses them. Whether either needs an account-level enable at all is **unverified** — the sandbox this was written in cannot reach Cloudflare's docs. Note that R2 turned out to need onboarding of exactly that kind, so do not assume these two don't. The first real provision run created three of four resources and reported
success. Two things were wrong with that.

The R2 listing failed with "A request to the Cloudflare API (/accounts/…/
r2/buckets) failed." and nothing else — wrangler puts the code that separates
a missing token scope from a product never enabled on the account on the line
under the marked one, and only the marked one was being read. The reason now
carries its continuation.

And the run went green while production was not ready: the provisioner exits
clean when it declines, which is right, but the preflight after it ran under
`|| true`. The preflight is the honest answer to "did it work"; it now decides
the run.

A concurrency group also queues a second press behind the first, so two runs
cannot both try to create the same resource.

Answers the C-SPAN licensing open question carried by both the market and
competitor wikis, and corrects the claim it supersedes.

C-SPAN's terms forbid any bot, spider or automatic device copying its content
without written permission, and it refuses unlicensed commercial use of its
programming even where the underlying federal event is public domain. The
chamber proceedings are public domain; C-SPAN's archive of them is not an
available source. The government publishes the same material itself —
HouseLive, Congress.gov video, and GPO's govinfo CREC bulk XML and API, whose
data Congress.gov states is public domain.

That backbone carries its own trap: the Congressional Record is not a
transcript. Members may correct their own remarks before publication and may
print material they never spoke on the floor, so a contradiction found between
two Record entries may be a contradiction between two edits.

Also records the substitute academics adopted after the Twitter API shutdown:
the Internet Archive TV News Archive plus GDELT, which splits the data vacuum —
broadcast speech is well-corpused and free, text and social speech are not.

and both deploy origins are readable off the deploys themselves — so neither
the per-resource dashboard clicking nor the two-pass first deploy was ever
necessary. A `provision` workflow now creates whatever the preflight reports

Phase 7 of #34, over the same ingestion chain the cron uses. Slices are
independent, so one bad slice costs one retry rather than a restart; and a
retried step reads what the previous attempt stored in R2 rather than
re-fetching, because the platform re-runs a whole step and every fetch inside

window. The slice size stays an unchecked bet against Cloudflare's Workflow

Phase 6 of #34. Pure functions over a series — no store, no model — so a case
can plant a step change or an outlier and assert exactly what comes back.

An anomaly is one utterance out of step, carrying where it was said and to whom.
A trend change reports the interval the step falls in, never a date; without
both ends dated there is no interval and nothing is recorded.

Two things the cases found. The leave-one-out baseline alone reported every point
of a bimodal series as an anomaly — and a bimodal series is what a trend change
looks like — so an anomaly now also has to be alone. And withUtterance collapsed
an explicit null date into its default, which is the failure 1.3 and 1.9 exist to
prevent, sitting in the fixtures.

The third leaf is the silence: a flat series, one too short to have a shape, and
one that drifts without stepping must all come back empty.

Acquisition called ensureFigure for every speaker an extractor named, so the
roster was whatever got crawled: a committee protocol's witnesses, petitioners

Who we track is now a committed file. syncRoster is the only path that creates

the file is refused rather than the entry.

repository is, until the defamation-law review in #28 has landed.

The rest of #34 phase 3's data model, additive beside everything v1 shipped.

A cluster is a row an utterance can open, so the corpus can be about something
new without any vocabulary being edited; its label is regenerated and display
only. A stance is a recorded judgment rather than something read off the
embedding, carrying the model and prompt that produced it, and a re-judgment
writes its own row rather than replacing one. A finding supersedes rather than
overwrites, and the table refuses one missing the attribute its kind turns on —
an anomaly without a venue, a trend change without an interval.

Also corrects the design's anomaly paragraph, which still said the attestation
carries venue and audience.

The deploy applies migrations before it replaces the Worker, so for the
length of a deploy the previous code serves against the new schema. An
additive change survives that window; a drop, a rename or a newly-required
column does not.

The gate rejects those three shapes unless the file declares itself the
contract step of an expand an earlier migration named. It checks files, so
it can insist a contract is a later file than its own expand; it cannot see
whether the three steps landed as three merges, and says so.

# hitbut's own build: the requirements suite, and the deploy that ships `main`.
name: product

on:
  pull_request:
  push:
    branches: [main]
  workflow_dispatch:

concurrency:
  group: product-${{ github.ref }}
  cancel-in-progress: true

jobs:
  checks:
    name: requirements (logic, behavior, server)
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v5
      - uses: actions/setup-node@v5
        with:
          node-version: 22
          cache: npm
      - run: npm ci
      - run: npm run typecheck
      # Watch the count, not the colour: a run that finds no tests exits green.
      - run: npm test
      - run: npm run test:server
      # Phase 0's exit condition that needs no account: the committed wrangler.toml
      # builds and its bindings resolve.
      - run: npx wrangler deploy --dry-run --outdir "$RUNNER_TEMP/dry-run"

  screen:
    name: requirements (screen)
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    # Pinned to the Playwright the goldens were rendered with. A different build
    # rasterises text differently, and the comparison would measure the renderer.
    container: mcr.microsoft.com/playwright:v1.56.1-noble
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v5
      - uses: actions/setup-node@v5
        with:
          node-version: 22
          cache: npm
      - run: npm ci
      - run: npm run test:screen
      - name: The pictures, when they disagree
        if: failure()
        # v6, not v5 like the actions above: upload-artifact's v5 still runs on
        # Node 20, so matching the others here would leave the deprecation in
        # place on the one step that only runs when something is already wrong.
        uses: actions/upload-artifact@v6
        with:
          name: screen-failures
          path: dev/requirements/failures/
          if-no-files-found: ignore

  deploy:
    name: ship main
    if: github.ref == 'refs/heads/main' && github.event_name != 'pull_request'
    needs: [checks, screen]
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    env:
      CLOUDFLARE_API_TOKEN: ${{ secrets.CLOUDFLARE_API_TOKEN }}
      CLOUDFLARE_ACCOUNT_ID: ${{ secrets.CLOUDFLARE_ACCOUNT_ID }}
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v5
      - uses: actions/setup-node@v5
        with:
          node-version: 22
          cache: npm
      - name: Is there an account to deploy to yet?
        id: account
        run: |
          if [ -z "$CLOUDFLARE_API_TOKEN" ] || [ -z "$CLOUDFLARE_ACCOUNT_ID" ]; then
            echo "Cloudflare provisioning (issue #27) has not landed — nothing to deploy yet."
            echo "ready=false" >> "$GITHUB_OUTPUT"
          else
            echo "ready=true" >> "$GITHUB_OUTPUT"
          fi
      - if: steps.account.outputs.ready == 'true'
        run: npm ci
      # Turns "the deploy failed somewhere in wrangler" into a named missing resource.
      # Everything it can report missing is one run of the *provision* workflow away.
      - name: Does production exist?
        if: steps.account.outputs.ready == 'true'
        run: npm run preflight
      - name: Bring the corpus schema up to date
        if: steps.account.outputs.ready == 'true'
        run: npm run corpus:migrate:remote
      # Each deploy step reads its origin back and exports it, so the site is built against
      # the API that was just deployed and the smoke test knows where to look. A repository
      # variable is an override for a custom domain, not something the first deploy needs.
      - name: Deploy the Worker
        if: steps.account.outputs.ready == 'true'
        env:
          API_ORIGIN: ${{ vars.API_ORIGIN }}
        run: npm run deploy:api
      - name: Build the site against the deployed API
        if: steps.account.outputs.ready == 'true'
        run: VITE_API_ORIGIN="$API_ORIGIN" npm run build:site
      - name: Deploy the site
        if: steps.account.outputs.ready == 'true'
        env:
          SITE_ORIGIN: ${{ vars.SITE_ORIGIN }}
        run: npm run deploy:site
      # Everything the suite proves is proven against a local workerd. This is the only
      # step that reads what actually shipped.
      - name: Does what shipped answer?
        if: steps.account.outputs.ready == 'true'
        run: npm run smoke

{"number":32,"title":"Reconnaissance and the first two sources","body":"Phase 4 of #25 left the concrete sources to a `map-a-data-source` reconnaissance and the owner's pick. This is that work. The roster it feeds is #31; the two must land together, because the first crawl is when an unrostered speaker first appears.

## The pair to start with, and why it is a pair

An inconsistency needs two moments about one topic, so two archives of the same era buy nothing. The minimum useful combination is one deep historical source and one current one, covering the same people:

1. **Knesset plenum and committee protocols — the "then".** Verbatim, attributed, dated, officially published, decades deep, and no contract to breach. Nothing else in Israeli public life gives all four for free.
2. **One current official feed — the "now".** gov.il and ministry announcements, or party press feeds. Announcement prose needs care on attribution: "the ministry said" is not "the minister said", and only the latter is a statement by a figure.

Deliberately **not** in the first pass: press interviews and op-eds (highest value for a stated position shift, worst on ToS and bot walls — they follow the legal review), broadcast (needs ASR), and social platforms. The last is not a scheduling call: the competitor-landscape wiki's clearest finding is that platform-API dependence is the top cause of death in this space — it killed both politician-tweet archives.

## Backfill window

**The current Knesset plus the previous one** — roughly four to six years. Far enough back that positions have genuinely moved, and a bounded job with an end, rather than an open-ended crawl. Ongoing coverage then runs on the cron, and the per-source `refreshMinutes` already in the registry carries the asymmetry: a protocol archive and a press feed do not move at the same speed.

## Reconnaissance needs a sanctioned home

**It cannot be done from an agent session.** The sandbox's egress policy denies `knesset.gov.il`, `www.gov.il` and `oknesset.org` outright — `403` to CONNECT at the proxy, a policy denial rather than a bot wall — and routing around a policy boundary is not on the table.

So the recon gets one home, which is also the shape the web-scraping rules ask for:

- [ ] A `workflow_dispatch` job on a GitHub runner that fetches a named list of candidate URLs and **commits the raw payloads** as sample fixtures.
- [ ] The `map-a-data-source` recon then runs **offline against those committed bytes**: locate the real data surface in the preferred order — a hydration blob, then a client API, then the markup — and write the findings into a reference doc beside the source module, complete enough that no question about the service needs a second probe.
- [ ] The parser and its per-source case are written against the same committed sample, so the extractor tests need no network and a parser fix costs no requests.
- [ ] Each source module declares its data surface and its refresh clock at registration, which the registry already enforces (`3.7`).

A datacenter IP being blocked is the expected failure here, not a surprise. If a source stays blocked from a runner, the answer is a commercial rendering proxy with the credential in repository secrets — one config-level decision in the fetch module, never a per-scraper workaround.

## Exit

The first two sources each have: a committed real sample, a reference doc, a registered module, and a passing case reading owner-reviewed expected values off the committed bytes. At that point the supported-source matrix becomes spec — each supported source its own leaf — and dropping one becomes a visible change rather than a silent regression.

Blocked on nothing. Needs #31's roster to land alongside it.

{"number":28,"title":"Honest gaps: what green in the requirements harness does not yet prove","body":"The banner on [`dev/requirements/requirements.md`](https://github.com/missingbulb/hitbut/blob/main/dev/requirements/requirements.md) points here. Green means every leaf is *claimed by a passing case of the right kind* — these are the places where that is honestly less than "verified in the world". Each is a burn-down item, not a caveat to live with.

**Four gaps are open.**

**1. The platform is a local one.** Server- and screen-kind cases run the shipped Worker on the real `workerd` runtime under Miniflare, against local D1 and R2. They confirm our code *asks* Cloudflare for the right thing — they do not confirm Cloudflare *performs* it: no real D1 (only the same SQLite engine), no real R2 durability, no edge cache, and no Workflow (the backfill's runner is a harness). Closes with #27 plus the post-deploy smoke #36 tracks.

**2. Requirement `7.1` is provisional.** "A merge to `main` reaches the deployed site with no human build step" cannot be asserted from a test at all; it is listed in `dev/requirements/provisional.json` so the coverage gate lets it stand unclaimed, and it is the one entry there. It burns down when provisioning lands and a merge is observed end to end.

**3. No embedding or stance model has been chosen, let alone evaluated for Hebrew.** This is what the old "the judge model is unevaluated for Hebrew" gap *became* — see the comment below. The pipeline runs against scripted fakes, which prove merge/embed/assign/place and the stored trail, and say nothing about judgment quality. A stance model placing Hebrew political speech on an axis is at least as sensitive to the language as a pairwise judge was. Blocked on #27; the model is a config value behind one interface, so a swap is not a rewrite.

**4. There is no supported-source matrix yet.** Acquisition and backfill are proven against a fixture source, which proves the machinery (raw-before-parse, retry policy, bot-wall detection, batch isolation, slice independence) and nothing about any real site. Real sources need a `map-a-data-source` recon and the owner's pick (#32); inventing a sample would prove support for a target the world does not serve, so none was invented.

**Two gaps have left this list.**

- **Israeli defamation law was unreviewed.** It has been reviewed. #54 landed what it requires: one written inclusion rule in `data/roster.json` that every entry must state how it meets, every quote naming the publication that carried it, and the detection caveat on the finding page itself. Until real people are in the roster, every figure in it is invented.
- **The pairwise judge is moot rather than closed.** #53 removed it; the concern moved into gap 3 above.

**It's already live.** The infrastructure question closed on 2026-08-24 (#27), and the last push to `main` (run [33522366478](https://github.com/missingbulb/hitbut/actions/runs/33522366478), 2026-09-01) deployed and smoke-tested green end to end:

- API — `https://hitbut-api.arielra.workers.dev` (D1 `hitbut-corpus` + R2 `hitbut-raw` bound, cron `23 */3 * * *` registered)
- Site — `https://hitbut.pages.dev`
- Smoke: 3/3 probes passed (corpus served, our 404 envelope, built site)

I could not re-confirm those two URLs from this session — this sandbox's egress proxy refuses them (`curl` returns `000`), and that's a policy boundary, not something to route around. The evidence above is the deploy job's own log.

So the real question is what's needed to see **something worth looking at** live. The corpus is empty by construction, in four places:

**1. No source is registered.** `productionRegistry()` in `src/backend/acquisition/registry.ts:99` returns an empty registry, so every cron pass fetches zero documents. This is [#32](https://github.com/missingbulb/hitbut/issues/32) — reconnaissance plus the first two sources (Knesset protocols as the "then", one official feed as the "now"). It needs a `workflow_dispatch` fetch job on a runner to commit raw samples, because agent sessions can't reach `knesset.gov.il` for the same policy reason as above.

**2. Every person in the roster is invented.** `data/roster.json` holds 3 fictional figures and says so; real names wait on the defamation review's roster pass ([#28](https://github.com/missingbulb/hitbut/issues/28), roster work is #31). Until that lands, a live site with real data isn't legally shippable.

**3. No models are wired.** `src/backend/index.ts:35` passes `UNPROVISIONED_EMBEDDER / VECTORS / STANCE`, so even with documents flowing, nothing gets embedded, clustered, or placed on a stance axis — each pass just records "capability unreachable". Needs the model choice ([#34](https://github.com/missingbulb/hitbut/issues/34)), then a `VECTORIZE_DIMENSIONS` repository variable and a re-run of *provision* to create the `hitbut-utterances` index (deliberately deferred in #27; the dimension is fixed at creation).

**4. Nothing names a cluster**, so subject chips render empty ([#33](https://github.com/missingbulb/hitbut/issues/33)).

Ordering: #32 + #31 first (real quotes on the page is the visible change; the site renders a corpus without any model), then #34 → Vectorize → #33 for the inconsistency lens on top.

> ⚠️ Still open: hitbut is deployed and answering, but empty — no registered sources (#32), an invented roster pending #31/#28, no embedding or stance model (#34, plus the Vectorize index #27 left uncreated), and no cluster naming (#33). Live URLs unverifiable from this session; the proxy denies them.

# Owner interaction preferences

Personal preferences from the repo owner for how the assistant should interact — tone, summary style, end-of-turn conventions, how results and decisions are surfaced, and the phrases the owner uses to trigger defined commands. These are **not** project conventions (those live in the [packs/](https://github.com/missingbulb/Claudinite/tree/main/packs) corpus, each pack bundling its skills); they're how the owner likes to be worked with. Where a preference triggers a command whose mechanics are a project convention, the mechanics stay in their own doc and the entry here just owns the trigger phrase.

## Preferences

- **End every turn with a blockquote callout** — `> ✅ All done`, or `> ⚠️ Still open: …` listing what remains — never hedged in prose.
- **"LGTM"** merges the change at hand into `main` (`merge-to-main` skill); it approves that change only, never later work.
- **"bump version"** raises the project's version; the project's own workflow decides how it changes and which files change.
- **In the conversation**: link every source-controlled document you edit, display every image you edit, link every issue/PR number.
- **Ask every decision or approval through an `AskUserQuestion` popup, never prose** — one question per item, each with its case.
- **Enclose anything the owner will lift elsewhere** — a prompt, a message, copy to paste — in one delimited block, boundaries unmistakable.
- **Prefix a prompt for another session, inside its block, with a disclaimer**: Claude wrote it — examine inconsistencies, don't follow blindly.
- **Open a pull request right after committing to a branch**, unasked — overriding Claude Code's default of waiting to be told.
- **When handing over a PR to review, describe the folders the change touched in the conversation, in a text box** — a brief line per folder saying what changed there. Show non-test folders only, and ignore README files, comment-only changes, and history-keeping updates (a version bump, a changelog or `VERSIONS.md` row).
- **Keep working through a multi-step plan without pausing for approval of each step** — aggregate the steps into one substantial change to review, and stop only for an action that reaches the world (a release, a fleet-wide effect, anything irreversible) or a decision only the owner can make.
- **Never schedule a self check-in to poll a PR** — no recurring wake-up, routine, or `send_later` re-arm that re-reads a PR's state, CI or mergeability on a timer. Act on PR events when they arrive; when nothing has arrived, end the turn.

- growth-dedup: Prune a repo's local packs of items the mounted Claudinite canon now covers — remove, strip to residue, or track a wording drift, never grow an entry. Use when the growth dedup task runs, or when asked to reconcile or dedup local packs against the canon.
- improve-comments: Improve the comments in a repo's own source — delete the ones that restate the code or narrate a past edit, correct the ones that have drifted from what the code now does, and add the why where only a reader's guess carries it. Use when working a repo's comments as their own pass (the tidy-repo pack's improve-comments task), never as a side effect of another change.

Use when adding a new source to a scraper, or when an existing source stops parsing and you suspect the site changed shape.

# Map a data source before you parse it

This runs **once per source** (and again when a site is redesigned). Its output is
not code — it is a committed reference doc plus one saved raw payload. Everything
after it is ordinary parsing.

## 1. Fetch one page and look at what came back

Save the raw response of a single representative page to disk and read it. You are
answering one question: **is the data in this document?**

- If the interesting rows are present in the markup, you have a server-rendered page
  — go to step 2.
- If you got a small shell (a few KB of script tags and an empty root), the page is a
  single-page app and the data arrives separately — go to step 3.

## 2. Look for a hydration blob first

A server-rendered app framework almost always embeds the exact object it rendered
from in a script tag with a stable id. Search the saved document for a large inline
JSON payload and find the path to the record you want (it is usually nested a few
levels under a props/data wrapper).

If one exists, **this is the surface**: it is the site's own typed record, one regex
and one JSON parse away, and it does not care about the layout. Save that object,
verbatim, as your first committed fixture.

If there is no blob, the page's self-describing metadata (JSON-LD `<script
type="application/ld+json">`, `og:` meta tags) is the next-best target — it survives
redesigns that break element selectors.

## 3. Find the client API

Identify the request the page makes for its rows. Two ways in, and the second one
matters more than it sounds:

- **Watch the page load** in browser devtools and read the request: URL, method,
  headers, auth, and the response shape.
- **Read the site's own JavaScript bundles.** Fetch the page, extract the script
  `src` paths (mind any asset prefix — the paths in the HTML already carry it),
  download them, and search for the operation names, query documents and field
  selections. For a GraphQL client the embedded query strings unescape into readable
  SDL, giving you the **complete** set of operations and fields the client was built
  against — the authoritative surface, short of introspection.

  This path is worth knowing because it needs **only the public site host**. When the
  API host is blocked from where you are but the site itself loads, reading its
  bundle still tells you exactly what a request would look like. It cannot execute
  anything, so it is not a bypass of the block.

Then note the auth story. A public listing is frequently reachable with anonymous
credentials the client itself ships — the same read access every visitor has. If
reaching the data requires a real account, stop and take that to the owner.

## 4. Probe the shape, not just the happy path

Before declaring the surface mapped, ask these of it explicitly, because each one has
silently corrupted a pipeline that assumed otherwise:

- **Are timestamps UTC or local?** Take one item whose real-world time you can verify
  independently and check.
- **Which field is authoritative for state?** If there is both a status enum and a
  summarizing boolean, find an item where they disagree — there usually is one.
- **What are the enum's legal values?** Take them from the service's own options
  endpoint, not from the sample you happened to pull.
- **Are numbers numbers?** Amounts and counts frequently arrive as strings.
- **Is anything missing from this surface entirely?** A listing endpoint often
  carries flags but no amounts, with the real values behind a separate per-item
  query. Find that out now, not after you've shipped a catalogue of nulls.
- **Is there a bulk form?** If the per-item query has no list variant, check whether
  one *request* can still carry many items (GraphQL aliases, a multi-id parameter).

## 5. Write it down, then stop

Commit a reference doc beside the scripts holding: the endpoint(s) and auth, the
field surface, the enum values, each answer from step 4, and — explicitly — the
questions you could **not** answer and where they'd have to come from. State the
access constraint too: which hosts are reachable from where, and which sanctioned job
is allowed to do the fetching.

The bar: **a later session should be able to write the parser from this doc without
touching the live service.** If it can't, the reconnaissance isn't finished.

input.title: A sanctioned fetch job for source reconnaissance samples
input.body:
The first checkbox of #32, and the thing everything else about real sources waits on.

Reconnaissance cannot be done from an agent session: the sandbox's egress policy denies `knesset.gov.il` and `www.gov.il` outright, and routing around a policy boundary is not on the table. So the fetching gets one sanctioned home — a `workflow_dispatch` job on a GitHub runner that fetches a committed list of candidate URLs and **commits the raw payloads**, after which the `map-a-data-source` recon runs offline against those bytes and needs no further requests.

## What lands

- `dev/samples/candidates.json` — the committed list: per candidate an id, the URL, what surface we expect to find, and what question it is meant to answer. Editing this file and re-dispatching is how the second round of recon (a page's script bundles, an endpoint the first round revealed) gets fetched.
- `dev/tools/fetch-samples.ts` — runs the list through the shipped `acquisition/fetcher.ts`, so the browser headers, the politeness delay, the retry policy and the bot-wall detection are the product's, not a second copy. Writes each payload under `dev/samples/payloads/`, skips what is already there unless `--force`, and records per-candidate outcome.
- `dev/samples/report.GENERATED.md` — what came back per candidate: status, bytes, a content sniff, and the failure reason where there was one. A datacenter IP being blocked is an expected outcome here, not a run failure.
- `.github/workflows/fetch-samples.yml` — the dispatch, which commits the payloads on a branch and opens a PR, so raw third-party bytes enter the repo through review.

## Why it exits clean on a blocked source

A source that refuses us is a finding for a human, not a broken pipeline — the run records the reason per candidate, keeps going, and finishes successfully with the report. What turns a `403` into a decision is the report, and the decision (a commercial rendering proxy with its credential in repository secrets, or dropping the candidate) is one config-level change in the fetch module.

## Exit

One dispatch has run, its PR carries real payloads for at least the Knesset protocol surface and one gov.il feed, and the report names what each candidate answered or refused. The recon doc and the parser are then #32's remaining work, offline.

Refs #32, #25

{"id":5217836716,"number":32,"state":"open","locked":false,"title":"Reconnaissance and the first two sources","body":"Phase 4 of #25 left the concrete sources to a `map-a-data-source` reconnaissance and the owner's pick. This is that work. The roster it feeds is #31; the two must land together, because the first crawl is when an unrostered speaker first appears.

## The pair to start with, and why it is a pair

An inconsistency needs two moments about one topic, so two archives of the same era buy nothing. The minimum useful combination is one deep historical source and one current one, covering the same people:

1. **Knesset plenum and committee protocols — the "then".** Verbatim, attributed, dated, officially published, decades deep, and no contract to breach. Nothing else in Israeli public life gives all four for free.
2. **One current official feed — the "now".** gov.il and ministry announcements, or party press feeds. Announcement prose needs care on attribution: "the ministry said" is not "the minister said", and only the latter is a statement by a figure.

Deliberately **not** in the first pass: press interviews and op-eds (highest value for a stated position shift, worst on ToS and bot walls — they follow the legal review), broadcast (needs ASR), and social platforms. The last is not a scheduling call: the competitor-landscape wiki's clearest finding is that platform-API dependence is the top cause of death in this space — it killed both politician-tweet archives.

## Backfill window

**The current Knesset plus the previous one** — roughly four to six years. Far enough back that positions have genuinely moved, and a bounded job with an end, rather than an open-ended crawl. Ongoing coverage then runs on the cron, and the per-source `refreshMinutes` already in the registry carries the asymmetry: a protocol archive and a press feed do not move at the same speed.

## Reconnaissance needs a sanctioned home

**It cannot be done from an agent session.** The sandbox's egress policy denies `knesset.gov.il`, `www.gov.il` and `oknesset.org` outright — `403` to CONNECT at the proxy, a policy denial rather than a bot wall — and routing around a policy boundary is not on the table.

So the recon gets one home, which is also the shape the web-scraping rules ask for:

- [ ] A `workflow_dispatch` job on a GitHub runner that fetches a named list of candidate URLs and **commits the raw payloads** as sample fixtures.
- [ ] The `map-a-data-source` recon then runs **offline against those committed bytes**: locate the real data surface in the preferred order — a hydration blob, then a client API, then the markup — and write the findings into a reference doc beside the source module, complete enough that no question about the service needs a second probe.
- [ ] The parser and its per-source case are written against the same committed sample, so the extractor tests need no network and a parser fix costs no requests.
- [ ] Each source module declares its data surface and its refresh clock at registration, which the registry already enforces (`3.7`).

A datacenter IP being blocked is the expected failure here, not a surprise. If a source stays blocked from a runner, the answer is a commercial rendering proxy with the credential in repository secrets — one config-level decision in the fetch module, never a per-scraper workaround.

## Exit

The first two sources each have: a committed real sample, a reference doc, a registered module, and a passing case reading owner-reviewed expected values off the committed bytes. At that point the supported-source matrix becomes spec — each supported source its own leaf — and dropping one becomes a visible change rather than a silent regression.

Blocked on nothing. Needs #31's roster to land alongside it.

This is that work. The roster it feeds is #31; the two must land together, because the first crawl is when an unrostered speaker first appears.

## The pair to start with, and why it is a pair

An inconsistency needs two moments about one topic, so two archives of the same era buy nothing. The minimum useful combination is one deep historical source and one current one, covering the same people:

1. **Knesset plenum and committee protocols — the "then".** Verbatim, attributed, dated, officially published, decades deep, and no contract to breach. Nothing else in Israeli public life gives all four for free.
2. **One current official feed — the "now".** gov.il and ministry announcements, or party press feeds. Announcement prose needs care on attribution: "the ministry said" is not "the minister said", and only the latter is a statement by a figure.

Deliberately **not** in the first pass: press interviews and op-eds (highest value for a stated position shift, worst on ToS and bot walls — they follow the legal review), broadcast (needs ASR), and social platforms. The last is not a scheduling call: the competitor-landscape wiki's clearest finding is that platform-API dependence is the top cause of death in this space — it killed both politician-tweet archives.

## Backfill window

**The current Knesset plus the previous one** — roughly four to six years. Far enough back that positions have genuinely moved, and a bounded job with an end, rather than an open-ended crawl. Ongoing coverage then runs on the cron, and the per-source `refreshMinutes` already in the registry carries the asymmetry: a protocol archive and a press feed do not move at the same speed.

## Reconnaissance needs a sanctioned home

**It cannot be done from an agent session.** The sandbox's egress policy denies `knesset.gov.il`, `www.gov.il` and `oknesset.org` outright — `403` to CONNECT at the proxy, a policy denial rather than a bot wall — and routing around a policy boundary is not on the table.

So the recon gets one home, which is also the shape the web-scraping rules ask for:

- [ ] A `workflow_dispatch` job on a GitHub runner that fetches a named list of candidate URLs and **commits the raw payloads** as sample fixtures.
- [ ] The `map-a-data-source` recon then runs **offline against those committed bytes**: locate the real data surface in the preferred order — a hydration blob, then a client API, then the markup — and write the findings into a reference doc beside the source module, complete enough that no question about the service needs a second probe.
- [ ] The parser and its per-source case are written against the same committed sample, so the extractor tests need no network and a parser fix costs no requests.
- [ ] Each source module declares its data surface and its refresh clock at registration, which the registry already enforces (`3.7`).

A datacenter IP being blocked is the expected failure here, not a surprise. If a source stays blocked from a runner, the answer is a commercial rendering proxy with the credential in repository secrets — one config-level decision in the fetch module, never a per-scraper workaround.

## Exit

The first two sources each have: a committed real sample, a reference doc, a registered module, and a passing case reading owner-reviewed expected values off the committed bytes. At that point the supported-source matrix becomes spec — each supported source its own leaf — and dropping one becomes a visible change rather than a silent regression.

Blocked on nothing. Needs #31's roster to land alongside it.

# Fetches the committed candidate URLs and opens a PR with what came back.
#
# This is the only place hitbut reaches a candidate source from. Agent sessions are denied
# these hosts by their egress policy, so reconnaissance is split in two: this job gets the
# bytes into the repo, and every question about a source is then answered offline against
# them. Re-dispatching after editing `dev/samples/candidates.json` is how the next round —
# a page's script bundles, an endpoint the first round revealed — gets fetched.
#
# A button rather than a schedule: nothing here needs to be current, and a recurring crawl
# of sites we are asking a favour of is the traffic most likely to get us blocked.
name: fetch-samples

on:
  workflow_dispatch:
    inputs:
      force:
        description: 'Re-fetch candidates whose payload is already committed'
        type: boolean
        default: false
      only:
        description: 'Comma-separated candidate ids, or blank for all of them'
        type: string
        default: ''

# Two runs fetching the same list would race each other into the same branch and spend the
# requests twice for one answer.
concurrency:
  group: fetch-samples
  cancel-in-progress: false

permissions:
  contents: write
  pull-requests: write

jobs:
  fetch:
    name: fetch the candidate list
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v5
      - uses: actions/setup-node@v5
        with:
          node-version: 22
          cache: npm
      - run: npm ci
      - name: Fetch what is missing
        run: npm run fetch-samples ${{ inputs.force && '-- --force' || '' }} ${{ inputs.only && format('-- --only {0}', inputs.only) || '' }}
      # Raw bytes from a third party enter the repo through review, not straight to main:
      # what they contain is exactly what nobody has read yet.
      - name: Open a PR with what came back
        env:
          GH_TOKEN: ${{ github.token }}
        run: |
          if git diff --quiet -- dev/samples; then
            echo "Nothing new came back — no payload changed. The log above says what each"
            echo "candidate answered; a run where everything was already saved is a no-op."
            exit 0
          fi
          branch="samples/run-${{ github.run_id }}"
          git config user.name "github-actions[bot]"
          git config user.email "41898282+github-actions[bot]@users.noreply.github.com"
          git checkout -b "$branch"
          git add dev/samples
          git commit -m "Reconnaissance samples from run ${{ github.run_id }}

          Refs #208, #32"
          git push -u origin "$branch"
          gh pr create \
            --title "Reconnaissance samples from run ${{ github.run_id }}" \
            --body "Raw payloads fetched by [fetch-samples](https://github.com/missingbulb/hitbut/actions/runs/${{ github.run_id }}), for the reconnaissance in #32 to read offline. What each candidate answered — including the ones that refused us — is in \`dev/samples/report.GENERATED.md\` in this diff.

          Refs #208, #32" \
            --base main \
            --head "$branch"

+# these hosts by their egress policy, so reconnaissance is split in two: this job gets the
+# bytes into the repo, and every question about a source is then answered offline against
+# them. Re-dispatching after editing `dev/samples/candidates.json` is how the next round —
+# a page's script bundles, an endpoint the first round revealed — gets fetched.
+#
+# A button rather than a schedule: nothing here needs to be current, and a recurring crawl
+# of sites we are asking a favour of is the traffic most likely to get us blocked.
+name: fetch-samples
+
+on:
+  workflow_dispatch:
+    inputs:
+      force:
+        description: 'Re-fetch candidates whose payload is already committed'
+        type: boolean
+        default: false
+      only:
+        description: 'Comma-separated candidate ids, or blank for all of them'
+        type: string
+        default: ''
+
+# Two runs fetching the same list would race each other into the same branch and spend the
+# requests twice for one answer.
+concurrency:
+  group: fetch-samples
+  cancel-in-progress: false
+
+permissions:
+  contents: write
+  pull-requests: write
+
+jobs:
+  fetch:
+    name: fetch the candidate list
+    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
+    steps:
+      - uses: actions/checkout@v5
+      - uses: actions/setup-node@v5
+        with:
+          node-version: 22
+          cache: npm
+      - run: npm ci
+      - name: Fetch what is missing
+        run: npm run fetch-samples ${{ inputs.force && '-- --force' || '' }} ${{ inputs.only && format('-- --only {0}', inputs.only) || '' }}
+      # Raw bytes from a third party enter the repo through review, not straight to main:
+      # what they contain is exactly what nobody has read yet.
+      - name: Open a PR with what came back
+        env:
+          GH_TOKEN: ${{ github.token }}
+        run: |
+          if git diff --quiet -- dev/samples; then
+            echo "Nothing new came back — no payload changed. The log above says what each"
+            echo "candidate answered; a run where everything was already saved is a no-op."
+            exit 0
+          fi
+          branch="samples/run-${{ github.run_id }}"
+          git config user.name "github-actions[bot]"
+          git config user.email "41898282+github-actions[bot]@users.noreply.github.com"
+          git checkout -b "$branch"
+          git add dev/samples
+          git commit -m "Reconnaissance samples from run ${{ github.run_id }}
+
+          Refs #208, #32"
+          git push -u origin "$branch"
+          gh pr create \
+            --title "Reconnaissance samples from run ${{ github.run_id }}" \
+            --body "Raw payloads fetched by [fetch-samples](https://github.com/missingbulb/hitbut/actions/runs/${{ github.run_id }}), for the reconnaissance in #32 to read offline. What each candidate answered — including the ones that refused us — is in \`dev/samples/report.GENERATED.md\` in this diff.
+
+          Refs #208, #32" \
+            --base main \
+            --head "$branch"

reconnaissance is the same move: when a page turns out to be a shell, its script bundle
paths become candidates, and reading them needs only the public site host.

archive. The corpus's own data does not come from here; it comes from the crawl, from
production.

input.body:
The first checkbox of #32: the one place allowed to fetch a candidate source, so that reconnaissance can then happen offline against bytes in the repo. Agent sessions are denied `knesset.gov.il` and `www.gov.il` by their egress policy, and that is a boundary to respect rather than route around.

## What this adds

- **`dev/samples/candidates.json`** — twelve candidate URLs across the two sources #32 picked: the Knesset OData surfaces (people, positions, plenum and committee sittings, the protocol documents, the service document itself, and the older v3 endpoint as a fallback), the human-facing sittings page, and three gov.il surfaces. Every line is a *hypothesis* — nothing in it has been reached from here — and each carries the question it is meant to answer.
- **`dev/tools/fetch-samples.ts`** — works the list through the shipped `acquisition/fetcher.ts`, so the browser headers, the randomised politeness delay, the retry policy and the anti-bot detection are the product's rather than a second copy. Saves each payload under `dev/samples/payloads/`, names the file by what the bytes *are* rather than what the candidate hoped for, skips what is already saved unless `--force`, and takes `--only` for one candidate.
- **`dev/samples/report.GENERATED.md`** — per candidate: saved, already saved, refused (with the reason) or not asked about, plus a preview of what came back. A `--only` run still reports the whole list from disk, so a partial run cannot erase the record.
- **`.github/workflows/fetch-samples.yml`** — the dispatch. It commits the payloads on a branch and opens a PR, because raw third-party bytes are exactly what nobody has read yet.

## Watching it work

The suite has no network, so the tool was rehearsed against a local server covering all four outcomes — a JSON body saved as `.json`, an HTML body as `.html`, an empty body and a 404 both recorded as refusals with the run still exiting clean — then the skip-on-rerun path, and `--only`/`--force`. `npx tsc --noEmit` and `npm test` (97 tests) are green.

What it cannot prove from here is whether any candidate URL is right; that is the dispatch's job, and a refusal is an answer the report is built to carry.

## Next

Dispatch [fetch-samples](https://github.com/missingbulb/hitbut/actions/workflows/fetch-samples.yml) once this merges. Its PR is what the `map-a-data-source` recon reads — and the Knesset person/position payloads are also how the real roster gets its 100 names from the Knesset's own record rather than from any model's memory of who currently holds a seat.

Closes #208
Refs #32
